blocks.lead: Premium vinyl plank buys you a thicker wear layer, a rigid core, deeper texture, longer planks and a real warranty. The installation labor is the same $2.50 per sq ft either way.
blocks.detail: Because Wills Flooring charges the same labor for any plank, the entire price difference between cheap and premium is material. That makes the decision simple: pay for the features your rooms will actually test, and skip the ones they will not.

blocks.html: Stand in the vinyl aisle of any Seattle big-box store and the planks look alike: same gray oak, same click edge, and a price spread of three or four times between the bottom shelf and the top. A common Reddit thread asks whether anyone can tell the difference once it is on the floor. On day one, no. In a Ballard rental after two winters of wet boots, or a Capitol Hill condo with a 90-pound dog, absolutely. Here is what the extra money buys, where it earns its keep in Seattle homes, and where it is wasted.

blocks.text: Where cheap plank fails first in Seattle homes

items.title: Entries and mudrooms
items.text: Wet grit from a Seattle sidewalk acts like sandpaper. A 6 mil wear layer at the front door of a busy Wallingford house shows a dull path in two or three winters. A 20 mil layer takes the same abuse for a decade.

items.title: Old, uneven subfloors
items.text: Craftsman and Tudor homes in Ballard, Queen Anne and West Seattle have fir subfloors that dip and hump. Thin flexible plank shows every ridge within months. Rigid core bridges the small stuff, though nothing replaces proper prep.

items.title: South-facing rooms
items.text: Budget flexible plank can expand and gap or lift in a sunroom or in front of a big south window. Rigid SPC is far more stable in heat and is the right pick for any room with all-day glass.

items.title: Dogs and rolling chairs
items.text: Claws and office chairs scuff a basic urethane finish quickly. Ceramic-bead coatings on premium planks resist that and keep a matte look. Dents from dropped pans are a core question: rigid cores shrug them off, soft cores do not.

blocks.text: Mistakes Seattle buyers make in the vinyl aisle

items: Judging by total thickness. An 8 mm plank with a 6 mil wear layer is a thick cheap floor. Thickness helps with dents and subfloor telegraphing; only the wear layer fights wear.
Buying the premium plank and skipping subfloor prep to pay for it. Flatness matters more than price; see how flat a subfloor needs to be.
Trusting a lifetime warranty without reading it. Many exclude wear in commercial-like use, sunlight, pet urine and any install not done to the letter of the spec.
Choosing the cheapest plank for a condo, then failing the HOA's sound test. Attached pad and an approved underlayment are part of the material cost in Capitol Hill and Belltown buildings.
Mixing tiers across a doorway. A premium great room next to a budget hallway shows the seam in texture and sheen.
Assuming premium means waterproof everywhere. Both tiers are water-resistant on top; neither stops water from getting under the floor at the edges.

blocks.title: The honest middle:
blocks.text: For most Seattle houses the sweet spot is a 12 to 20 mil wear layer, a rigid SPC core around 5.5 to 6.5 mm, and a plank at least 48 inches long with an attached pad. It costs meaningfully less than the top shelf and holds up in every room short of a commercial entry.
How to compare two planks in your own living room

items.html: Find the wear layer on the box or spec sheet. It is stated in mil. If a salesperson answers with total thickness in millimeters, ask again.
Do the key test. Drag a key across the sample with moderate pressure. Ceramic-bead finishes barely mark; basic urethane shows a white line.
Flex it. Bend the sample. Flexible plank folds like a floor mat. Rigid core resists and snaps back. Rigid is what you want over an old Seattle fir subfloor.

Look at it in your light, at floor level. Lay three samples on the floor at noon and again at night. Printed grain that repeats and a flat, shiny surface show up fast in real light and not at all in a showroom.
Drop something. A set of keys on a sample sitting on your subfloor tells you how the plank will sound. Attached pad changes it noticeably, which matters in a condo.
Get the tier named on the quote. Our written quote lists the exact product, wear layer and underlayment, plus installation at $2.50 per sq ft, so two bids can be compared line by line.

faq.q: Is expensive vinyl plank really better than cheap vinyl plank?
faq.a: In the ways that show up over time, yes. A thicker wear layer, rigid core and better surface coating mean the floor still looks new after years of Seattle grit and dog claws. On day one they look nearly identical, which is why the difference is invisible in the store and obvious five years later.

faq.q: What wear layer thickness should I buy?
faq.a: For a main floor with kids or pets, 20 mil is the safe choice. For bedrooms or a low-traffic home, 12 mil holds up well. Six to eight mil is rental-turnover material. Wear layer is the single spec that predicts how long the floor lasts, so decide it before color.

faq.q: Does Wills Flooring charge more to install premium vinyl plank?
faq.a: No. Installation is $2.50 per sq ft for any click or glue-down vinyl plank, with a 500 sq ft minimum and $100 per stair. The material is quoted separately based on what you choose, so upgrading tiers changes only the material line on your quote.

faq.q: Is cheap vinyl plank okay for a Seattle rental?
faq.a: Often, yes. If you expect to refresh the unit every few years, a mid or budget plank with a rigid core is sensible. Spend on the core rather than the wear layer, because old Seattle subfloors punish thin flexible plank faster than tenants wear through the finish.

faq.q: Does premium vinyl plank increase resale value in Seattle?
faq.a: It helps a listing read as move-in ready, especially with long, wide, textured planks in a warm neutral. Buyers in Ballard and Green Lake still prefer real hardwood at the top of the market, but convincing premium vinyl in a kitchen or basement is a plus, while a shiny, repeating budget plank is a negative.

faq.q: Can I mix cheap and premium plank in different rooms?
faq.a: Yes, if a doorway with a transition strip separates them. Different tiers rarely match in texture and sheen even in the same color name, so avoid running one into the other in an open plan. Budget plank in closets and a guest room with premium in the main living areas is a common and sensible split.
